overview.body:
**Bodhidharma** ​(*bodhidharma*) — ‌The Dharma ‌of Awakening, ​First ​Patriarch · ​Dharma of ​awakening ​— belongs ‌to the ​Chinese tradition, ​where ‌it is ​catalogued under ‌the ​domain "Zen ‌Patriarch, Wall-Gazer". ​The name ​means ​"Dharma of ​awakening"[^1].

**Bodhidharma** ​is ‌the First ​Patriarch of ‌Zen: the ​Indian ‌prince-turned-monk who ​crossed the ‌Pamirs ​to China ‌around 520 ​CE, sat ​facing ‌a wall ‌at Shaolin ‌for ​nine years, ​and transmitted ‌the Buddha’s ​wordless ​teaching outside ‌the scriptures. ​His ​legend is ‌the bridge ​between India ‌and ​East Asia ​— and ​the ​seed of ‌martial, meditative, ‌and cultural ​traditions ‌that span ​the continent.[^2]

​PuniCodex ‌restores the ‌name as ‌**Bodhidharma** and ‌serves ​its temple ‌at [its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/bodhidharma/). ​The restoration ​aSCII-equivalent form ‌— a ​description ​computed from ​the displayed ‌form ​itself. The ​plain ASCII ​form *bodhidharma* ‌survives ​as a ‌modern convenience ​imposed ‌by the ​early domain-name ‌system; the ‌restoration, ​not the ​fallback, is ​the ​form the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in Chinese ​characters ​as **菩提達磨**. ​Etymologically ​it ​means "Dharma ‌of ​awakening"[^1].

The ​ASCII ‌form *bodhidharma* ​survives ‌only because ​the ‌early domain-name ​system ​could not ​carry ​diacritics; it ​is ‌a ​technological compromise, ‌not ​an ancient ‌spelling. ​The Unicode ‌restoration ​**Bodhidharma** recovers ‌the ​full diacritic ​detail ‌of the ‌scholarly ‌transliteration directly ​in ​the ‌address bar. ​The ​restoration aSCII-equivalent ‌form ​— a ​description ‌computed from ​the ‌displayed form ​itself.

​The letter-by-letter ​transformation ​runs:

- **b** ‌→ ‌**B** ​— Same, ‌capitalized
- ​**o** → ​**o** ‌— Same
- ‌**d** ‌→ **d** ‌— ​Same
- **h** ‌→ ​**h** — ​Same
- ​**i** → ‌**i** ​— ​Same
- **d** ​→ ‌**d** — ​Same
- ​**h** → ​**h** ‌— Same

- **r** ​→ ‌**r** — ‌Same

pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is **/ˌboʊdɪˈdɑːrmə/** ​— ​Sanskrit ​→ ‌Chinese transmission ​(Pútídámó).[^1]

​Phoneme ‌by phoneme:

- ​**Bodhi-** ‌— ​From ‌Sanskrit bodhi, ​“awakening” ​— ​the name ​begins ​in ‌the ​Buddha’s own ‌enlightenment-word.
- ​**-dhar-** ‌— From ​√dhṛ, ‌“to ​hold, ‌sustain” — ​the ​same ‌root as ‌dharma’s ‌“that ​which ​holds”.
- **-ma** ‌— ​The ​Chinese rendered ‌it ​菩提達磨 ​(Pútídámó); ‌the Japanese, ​Daruma; ‌the ​West, ​Bodhidharma.

For ​the ​modern ‌speaker, the ‌closest ​approximation ‌is: ​“boh-dee-DAR-muh”

Kindred ​and ‌historical ‌forms of ‌the ‌name:

- ​**Chinese** ‌— Pútídámó ​菩提達磨 ​— ​the First ‌Patriarch
- ​**Japanese** ​— ​Daruma 達磨 ‌— ​the ​roly-poly doll ​is ‌his ​image

‌The name ​means ‌“awakening-perfection” ​or “dharma ‌of ‌awakening” ​— ​the Indian ​prince ​who ‌carried Zen ‌to ​China.

domains.body:
**Bodhidharma** ​is the ‌First Patriarch ‌of ​Zen: the ​Indian prince-turned-monk ​who crossed ​the ​Pamirs to ‌China around ​520 ​CE, sat ‌facing a ​wall ‌at Shaolin ​for nine ‌years, ​and transmitted ​the Buddha’s ​wordless teaching ​outside ​the scriptures. ‌His legend ​is ‌the bridge ​between India ‌and ​East Asia ‌— and ​the ‌seed of ​martial, meditative, ​and cultural ‌traditions ‌that span ‌the continent.[^1]

### ​The ​Wall-Gazing

Nine ‌years facing ​the ​wall at ‌Shaolin; the ​tradition’s ​image of ‌unmoving resolve ​— and ‌of ​the mind’s ​own wall.

### ​The ​First Patriarch

‌The twenty-eighth ‌Indian ​patriarch who ‌became China’s ​first ​— the ‌wordless transmission ‌passed through ‌him.

### ‌Daruma’s Eyes

​The legend: ‌he ​cut off ​his eyelids ​in ‌wrath at ​sleep — ​and ​where they ‌fell, tea ​plants grew. ​Japan’s ​doll watches ‌with one ​eye.

### ‌The Bone ​of the ‌Buddha

​His only ‌transmission: a ‌bowl, ​a robe, ​and a ​bone — ​the ‌mind-to-mind seal ‌outside the ​scriptures.

sources.citation: Blue Cliff Record (Hekiganroku), case 1.

symbols.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated with ‌Bodhidharma ​concentrates ​in ​a small ​set ​of ‌recurring attributes, ​each ​a ‌compressed ​statement about ‌the ​name:[^1]

- ‌**The ​Wall-Gazing** — ​Nine ​years ​facing the ​wall ‌at ​Shaolin; ‌the tradition’s ​image ‌of ​unmoving ‌resolve — ​and ‌of ​the mind’s ​own ‌wall.
- ‌**The ‌First Patriarch** ​— ​The ‌twenty-eighth ​Indian patriarch ​who ‌became ​China’s first ​— ‌the ​wordless ‌transmission passed ​through ​him.
- ​**Daruma’s ​Eyes** — ‌The ‌legend: ​he cut ‌off ​his ​eyelids ‌in wrath ‌at ‌sleep ‌— ​and where ‌they ​fell, ​tea plants ​grew. ‌Japan’s ​doll ​watches with ​one ‌eye.
- ​**The ​Bone of ​the ‌Buddha** ​— His ‌only ​transmission: ‌a ​bowl, a ‌robe, ‌and ​a ​bone — ​the ​mind-to-mind ‌seal outside ‌the ​scriptures.

mythology.body:
Bodhidharma’s mythology ​is a layer-cake of ‌history and legend: the ‌historical missionary of the ​early sixth century; the ​wall-gazer of the Zen ​records; the Shaolin temple’s ​patron of the martial ​arts; and Japan’s ‌round Daruma doll, whose ​blank eyes you fill ​in when your wish ‌comes true. The legend ​grew because the teaching ‌needed a body — ​and the body it ‌chose was defiant, ​foreign, and perfectly still.[^1]

### ​The Crossing to China ​(Transmission Records)

The Zen ​records send him to ​the court of the ‌Liang emperor Wudi — ​the great Buddhist patron ‌who asks, ‘what ​is the highest meaning ‌of the holy truth?’ ​and is told ‘vast ‌emptiness, nothing holy’. The ​emperor, scandalized, asks who ‌stands before him: ‘Don’t ​know’, says the future ​patriarch, and leaves ‌for the north. The ‌dialogue founded the Zen ‌interview-style in a single ​exchange.[^2]

### Nine Years, One ​Wall (Wall-Gazing Legend)

At ‌Shaolin he sat facing ​a wall nine years; ​legend adds that ‌in frustration at sleep ​he cut off his ​eyelids — and tea, ‌the meditator’s ally, sprang ​from where they fell. ‌Huike, his future successor, ​stood in the snow ​and cut off ​his own arm to ​prove his sincerity; Bodhidharma ‌accepted him and transmitted ‌the teaching. The tradition’s ​founding images are all ‌of this order: resolve ​measured in what one ​will lose.

### The ‌Temple and the Arts ‌(Shaolin Cycle)

The legend ‌that he taught the ‌Shaolin monks exercises to ​strengthen their meditation — ‌the seed of Shaolin ​kung fu — belongs ​to the later ​layers, but it fixed ‌his place in the ​martial imagination: the first ​patriarch as the first ​master of body-discipline. The ‌*Yi Jin Jing* muscle-classic ​attaches itself to his ​name.

### The Round ​Wish-Keeper (Daruma Doll)

Japan ‌made him a doll: ​round as the wall-sitter’s ‌robe, weighted to right ​itself — *nanakorobi yaoki*, ‌fall seven times, rise ​eight. You paint one ‌blank eye when ‌you make a wish, ​the other when it ​comes true. The fierce ​Indian master ended as ​Japan’s most cheerful household ‌god of perseverance, keeping ‌his scowl and his ​self-righting bottom.
